title: Partitioning, Repartition, Coalesce and Skew

concepts.heading: Partitions Decide Parallelism
concepts.body: A stage runs one task per partition, and a task occupies one core, so the partition count caps how many cores can work at once. Too few partitions leave cores idle and make each task hold a large share of data, which risks spilling or out-of-memory errors. Too many tiny partitions make scheduling overhead larger than the work. The tuning guide recommends 2-3 tasks per core and notes that Spark handles tasks as short as 200 ms well, so having more partitions than cores is safe. Partition counts come from three places. File scans pack input into partitions of up to `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes`, 128 MB by default. Wide operations such as `groupBy` and `join` create `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` partitions, 200 by default. And you set the number yourself with `repartition` or `coalesce`. Check `df.rdd.getNumPartitions()` and the Stages tab before tuning: the symptom (idle cores, one slow task, spilling) tells you which direction to move.

concepts.heading: repartition Versus coalesce
concepts.body: `repartition(n)` always performs a full shuffle. It can raise or lower the partition count and balances sizes; with columns, `repartition(n, "id")` hash-partitions so equal keys land together. `repartitionByRange` (hint `REPARTITION_BY_RANGE`) partitions by ranges of the column values instead of hashing. `coalesce(n)` merges existing partitions as a narrow dependency without a shuffle: going from 1000 to 100 partitions, each new partition claims 10 old ones. It can only lower the count, and asking for more than the current number leaves the DataFrame unchanged, with no error. Use `coalesce` to cheaply shrink after a selective filter, and `repartition` to grow or balance. The PySpark docs warn about a drastic `coalesce(1)`: the whole upstream computation may then run on one node, because the merge propagates into earlier steps. `repartition(1)` adds a shuffle but keeps the upstream work parallel. In SQL the hints `COALESCE`, `REPARTITION` and `REPARTITION_BY_RANGE` match these APIs, while `REBALANCE` exists only as a hint and needs AQE.

concepts.heading: Recognizing and Handling Data Skew
concepts.body: Hash partitioning sends every row with the same key to one partition. If 70% of rows share `country = 'US'`, then `df.repartition("country")` creates one oversized partition and the stage waits for a single straggler. In the Spark UI the signature is a maximum task duration or shuffle read size many times the median. Remedies: partition by a column with many evenly used values, use `repartition(n)` without columns for round-robin balance, add a random salt to the key, or rely on AQE. For sort-merge joins, AQE splits a partition into evenly sized tasks when it is larger than `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor` (5) times the median and also larger than `skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes` (256 MB). Both conditions must hold. Example: with a median of 100 MB, the factor limit is 500 MB, so a 400 MB partition is not skewed even though it passes 256 MB, while a 620 MB partition is. Skew handling is on by default when AQE is.

concepts.heading: Reducing Shuffle Volume
concepts.body: Shuffles write map output to disk and move it over the network, so they are among the most expensive steps. Reduce the data entering a wide operation instead of tuning around it. Filter rows and select only needed columns early, so less data is shuffled. Aggregate before a join when the join does not need row-level detail: partial aggregation happens per partition first, so joining 10 billion clicks reduced to one row per user and day shuffles far less than joining the raw clicks. Broadcast a small side so the large side is not shuffled at all. Avoid wide steps that add nothing, such as an extra `repartition`, `distinct` or a global `orderBy` that no consumer needs. With AQE on, small post-shuffle partitions are merged for you; with AQE off, lower `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` for small jobs, for example to 8 for 50 MB of data, because 200 tiny tasks cost more than they save. Raising the shuffle partition count helps when partitions are so big that they spill.

examPoints: `coalesce` is narrow, only reduces partitions and never errors when asked for more; `repartition` shuffles and can grow or balance; `coalesce(1)` can collapse upstream work into one task.
Skew in AQE needs both conditions: larger than factor (5) times the median and larger than 256 MB; one huge key shows as max task far above median in the Spark UI.
Cut shuffle volume by filtering early, aggregating before joins, broadcasting small sides and skipping needless repartition, distinct and global orderBy.

quiz.q: A DataFrame has 2,000 small partitions after a selective filter. The next steps are narrow, about 200 partitions are wanted, and equal sizes do not matter. Which call is cheapest?
choices: `df.repartition(200)`, because the full shuffle also balances the partition sizes for the steps that follow
`df.coalesce(200)`, which merges neighbouring partitions without a shuffle
`df.repartition(200, "id")`, which hash-partitions by key and is therefore cheaper than a round-robin shuffle of all rows
`df.sortWithinPartitions("id")`, because sorting inside each task lowers the number of partitions that exist
quiz.explain: Merging partitions as a narrow dependency avoids moving rows between executors. Both repartition forms shuffle everything, and a local sort never changes the partition count.

quiz.q: With AQE defaults (skew factor 5, threshold 256 MB), the shuffle for a sort-merge join has a median partition of 80 MB and other partitions of 300, 450 and 900 MB. Which are treated as skewed?
choices: All three, because each of them is larger than the 256 MB threshold on its own
Only 900 MB, because skew handling needs a partition above 10 times the median
None of them, because skew handling is limited to partitions that exceed 1 GB
450 MB and 900 MB, which exceed both 400 MB (5 x median) and 256 MB
quiz.explain: A partition must beat the factor limit of 5 x 80 = 400 MB and the 256 MB threshold. The 300 MB partition passes only the threshold; 450 and 900 MB pass both.

recap: Partitions equal tasks. coalesce merges without a shuffle and only shrinks; repartition shuffles and balances. Skew shows as one slow task; AQE splits partitions above 5 x median and 256 MB. Shrink shuffles by filtering, aggregating first and broadcasting.

title: Adaptive Query Execution, Logs and Memory Diagnosis

concepts.heading: What AQE Changes at Runtime
concepts.body: Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) is a Spark SQL feature that uses runtime statistics to pick a more efficient plan, enabled by default since Spark 3.2.0 and controlled by the umbrella setting `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled`. A normal plan is built before the query starts from estimates that are often wrong after filters, joins and user code. A shuffle ends a stage and writes map output, so Spark knows the true size of every shuffle partition when the stage finishes. AQE uses those numbers to re-optimize the stages that have not started yet. It does not cache stage output, add executors or rewrite the plan at analysis time, and it does not cancel work that already finished. Because it reacts at shuffle boundaries, a query without a shuffle gains nothing: the scan's partition count comes from `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes` (128 MB by default) and the file layout, so fix a bad scan with `repartition(n)` after reading or by writing better-sized files.

concepts.heading: Coalescing, Join Switching and Skew Splitting
concepts.body: AQE applies three main optimizations. Coalescing merges contiguous small post-shuffle partitions when `spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled` is true (the default). It starts from `spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.initialPartitionNum`, or `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` if that is unset, and can only reduce the count. With `parallelismFirst` true (the default) it ignores the 64 MB advisory size and respects only the 1 MB minimum, so a 30 MB aggregation can end in far fewer tasks than 200. Join switching turns a sort-merge join into a broadcast hash join when a side's runtime size is under `spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`, which defaults to `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`. Setting that static value to `-1` therefore also disables the runtime switch unless the adaptive one is set separately. Skew splitting breaks oversized sort-merge join partitions into even tasks. The docs advise a large initial partition number and letting Spark pick the final one, so one setting handles a 1 GB day and a 2 TB day.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing Out-of-Memory Failures
concepts.body: First find where memory ran out. If `collect()` aborts with a message about `spark.driver.maxResultSize` (default 1g), the serialized results exceeded the limit that protects the driver. Aggregate on the cluster, for example `groupBy("country").count()`, and collect only the small result. If tasks fail with `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` during a join, each reduce task builds a hash table for its share, so the simplest fix is more parallelism: raise `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` or `repartition(n)` first so every task's input is smaller. If a cluster manager kills executors for exceeding the container limit and the logs show no `OutOfMemoryError`, raise `spark.executor.memoryOverhead`, the non-heap memory that covers Python workers and native libraries; its default is executor memory times 0.10 (0.40 for non-JVM jobs on Kubernetes) with a 384 MiB floor, supported on YARN and Kubernetes. A task payload warning means a large driver-side object travels inside every task; send it once with a broadcast variable. The tuning guide treats tasks above about 20 KiB as worth optimizing.

concepts.heading: Reading Logs, the Spark UI and GC Evidence
concepts.body: Every application serves the Spark UI on port 4040 of the driver, with stages and tasks, storage, environment and executors. By default it vanishes when the application ends. To inspect past runs, set `spark.eventLog.enabled` to true with a shared `spark.eventLog.dir`, and point a Spark History Server at that directory with `spark.history.fs.logDirectory`; keeping the driver alive with a sleep loop is not the answer. Use the tabs to match symptoms: few tasks in the Stages tab with idle cores in the Executors tab is underutilization, such as a `coalesce(4)` placed before a slow UDF on a 32-core cluster, fixed by repartitioning to a multiple of the cores before the UDF. For garbage collection, add `-verbose:gc -XX:+PrintGCDetails` through `spark.executor.extraJavaOptions`; the output lands in the workers' stdout files, not on the driver. A full GC invoked several times before a task finishes means there is not enough memory for task execution. An old generation close to full means lowering `spark.memory.fraction` to cache less.

examPoints: AQE re-plans from shuffle-stage statistics: coalesces small partitions, switches sort-merge to broadcast hash join, splits skewed partitions; a plan without a shuffle gets no benefit.

Match the OOM to the fix: collect and maxResultSize means aggregate first; heap OOM in reduce tasks means more partitions; killed containers without OutOfMemoryError means memoryOverhead; large task payload means broadcast.
Past runs need `spark.eventLog.enabled` plus a History Server; GC logs sit on executors, and several full GCs per task mean too little execution memory.

quiz.q: A join is planned as sort-merge because Spark overestimates the size of one input. After the first shuffle stage a runtime statistic shows this side is only 5 MB. AQE is on with defaults. What can AQE do?
choices: Switch the remaining join to a broadcast hash join, since the runtime size is under the adaptive threshold
Keep the sort-merge join, because Spark fixes the join strategy before the first stage and never revises it while the query runs
Cancel the finished shuffle stage and restart the whole query so the small side is broadcast from the beginning of the plan
Replace the join with a cross join, because small inputs can be matched against every row of the large side
quiz.explain: AQE re-optimizes the stages that have not started, using real sizes from the shuffle. It does not restart finished work, and it never turns an equi-join into a cross join.

quiz.q: PySpark executors on Kubernetes are killed mid-stage for exceeding their pod memory limit. The executor logs show no OutOfMemoryError, and the job uses Python UDFs and native libraries. Which setting should be raised first?
choices: `spark.driver.maxResultSize`, which caps the serialized task results the driver accepts for one action
`spark.eventLog.compress`, which decides whether the event log is compressed before it reaches storage
`spark.executor.memoryOverhead`, the non-heap memory per executor
`spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes`, which sets the target size of shuffle partitions after coalescing
quiz.explain: The container limit is heap plus non-heap memory. Python workers and native libraries use the non-heap part, and the manager kills the process before the JVM can throw an error.

recap: AQE uses real shuffle statistics to coalesce, switch joins and split skew, but only at shuffle boundaries. Pick the OOM fix by location: driver result, task heap, container overhead, task size. Keep event logs and a History Server for past runs.

title: Structured Streaming Engine, Output Modes and Sinks

concepts.heading: The Programming Model
concepts.body: Structured Streaming treats a live stream as a table that keeps growing. You write the same DataFrame or SQL operations as for a batch query, and Spark runs them incrementally on the new rows, updating a result table. Many other engines make you maintain running aggregates and reason about delivery guarantees yourself; here Spark owns that work. Because a stream never ends, actions that return a result immediately do not work: `count()` raises an `AnalysisException`, so use `groupBy().count()`, which is a streaming DataFrame holding a running count. `show()` is replaced by the console sink, and `foreach()` by `writeStream.foreach`. `limit`, `take` and `distinct` are unsupported, and sorting is allowed only after an aggregation in complete mode. File-based sources require an explicit schema by default, so `spark.readStream.format("json").load(path)` fails until you pass `.schema(...)`, or set `spark.sql.streaming.schemaInference` to true for ad-hoc work. The schema stays consistent across restarts.

concepts.heading: Micro-Batches and Triggers
concepts.body: By default a query runs as a series of small batch jobs, a micro-batch engine with latencies down to about 100 ms and exactly-once guarantees. With no trigger, the next micro-batch starts as soon as the previous one completes. `trigger(processingTime="10 seconds")` starts batches at fixed intervals: if a batch finishes early, the engine waits for the boundary; if a 25-second batch misses boundaries, the next one starts immediately after it, with no parallel catch-up and no dropped data. With no new data, no batch is started. `trigger(availableNow=True)` processes everything available, possibly in several micro-batches, then stops, which suits periodic runs that start and stop a cluster. The one-time trigger is deprecated in favor of availableNow, and availableNow is the one to pick. A continuous trigger exists for roughly 1 ms latency but is experimental and gives only at-least-once guarantees, so it is not the way to get exactly-once.

concepts.heading: Fault Tolerance and Exactly-Once
concepts.body: End-to-end exactly-once needs three parts. The source must be replayable, with offsets such as Kafka offsets, so the same range can be read again. The engine records the offset range of each trigger in write-ahead logs inside the `checkpointLocation`, along with running aggregate state; the path must be on an HDFS-compatible, fault-tolerant file system. The sink must be idempotent, so writing a batch twice leaves the same result. After a driver crash, restarting the same code with the same checkpoint resumes after the last committed batch with its saved state and re-runs any batch that was planned but not completed. A new empty checkpoint directory starts a fresh query. A checkpoint alone is not enough: the socket source is meant for testing and is not fault-tolerant because the data cannot be read again, so production needs a replayable source such as Kafka or files. The console and memory sinks are also not fault-tolerant, because they do not guarantee persistence.

concepts.heading: Output Modes and Sinks
concepts.body: Append mode is the default and writes only new rows, valid when rows never change later. Complete writes the whole result table each trigger and supports aggregations. Update writes only rows changed since the last trigger; without aggregation it equals append. An aggregation without a watermark supports complete and update, not append, because counts can still change. Example: batch 1 has devices A, A, B and prints A=2 and B=1; batch 2 adds A and C, so update mode prints A=3 and C=1, leaving B out, while complete prints A=3, B=1 and C=1. The file sink supports append only and is exactly-once, so an unwatermarked aggregation cannot be written to Parquet directly. Kafka and foreach sinks are at-least-once. `foreachBatch` receives each micro-batch DataFrame and a batch id, lets you use batch writers such as JDBC, and by default gives at-least-once; use the batch id to skip or upsert batches already written. Console and memory sinks are for debugging on small data.

examPoints: Streaming DataFrames use batch APIs but not actions: `count()`, `show()` and `limit` fail, `groupBy().count()` plus a sink works, and file sources need a schema.

Exactly-once needs a replayable source, a checkpoint with write-ahead logs and an idempotent sink; the socket source, console and memory sinks are not fault-tolerant, and continuous mode is experimental at-least-once.
An unwatermarked aggregation allows only complete or update; the file sink allows only append; foreachBatch is at-least-once unless the batch id is used to deduplicate.

quiz.q: A query counts events per device with `events.groupBy("device").count()` and writes to Parquet files with the file sink. No watermark is defined. What happens?
choices: It runs and rewrites the full result table in complete mode at every trigger, because the file sink selects the mode itself
It runs in update mode and appends only the changed counts to new files, because update is the file sink default
It is rejected, because the file sink supports only append and an unwatermarked aggregation cannot use append
It runs once the trigger is set to `availableNow`, because file output needs a finite amount of input
quiz.explain: Mode support must overlap. The aggregation allows only complete and update, and the file sink allows only append, so no mode is valid.

quiz.q: A team wants end-to-end exactly-once results after any failure and restart. Which combination delivers it?
choices: A replayable source, an idempotent sink and a checkpoint
A socket source with a console sink and a trigger short enough that no data arrives between two micro-batches
Any source with a sink that compares its final table with the input and repairs differences after the restart
A continuous trigger with any sink, since that mode has the lowest latency and so the strongest delivery guarantee
quiz.explain: Offsets let the engine re-read the same range, the write-ahead log records what each trigger covered, and an idempotent sink makes a repeated write harmless. Continuous mode is experimental and at-least-once.

recap: A stream is an unbounded table queried with batch APIs, minus immediate actions. Checkpoint, replayable source and idempotent sink give exactly-once. Pick output modes by query type and sink: the file sink is append only, aggregations without a watermark are complete or update.

title: Windows, Watermarks and Streaming Deduplication

concepts.heading: Windows on Event Time
concepts.body: Selection and projection work on streams as in batch: `select`, `where` and `withColumn` are stateless, so the output modes append and update behave the same. Aggregations are stateful. Event-time windows group by the time inside the data, not the arrival time. A tumbling window, `window("ts", "10 minutes")`, has fixed, non-overlapping intervals, so each event falls in exactly one. A sliding window, `window("ts", "10 minutes", "5 minutes")`, has a slide shorter than its length, so windows overlap and one event is counted in several. An event at 12:07 belongs to 12:00-12:10 and 12:05-12:15, but not to 12:10-12:20. A session window, `session_window("ts", "5 minutes")`, has a dynamic size: it extends while events arrive within the gap and closes after silence, which fits bursts of user activity of different lengths. In streaming, session windows do not support update mode, and the grouping key needs at least one more column besides the session window, such as the user.

concepts.heading: Watermarks and Late Data
concepts.body: State for windows would grow forever without a rule for when an old window is final. A watermark supplies it: `withWatermark("ts", "10 minutes")` sets the watermark to the largest event time seen minus the threshold, and it only moves forward. If the engine sees an event at 12:14, the watermark becomes 12:04 for the next trigger; when it reaches 12:11, the state of window 12:00-12:10 is dropped and later records for it are ignored as too late. In update mode counts are written as they change. In append mode a window is emitted once, only after the watermark passes its end, so output is delayed by the threshold. Conditions for state cleanup: the output mode is append or update, since complete keeps everything; `withWatermark` is called on the same event-time column the aggregation uses; and it is called before the aggregation. `df.groupBy("ts").count().withWatermark("ts", "1 minute")` has the order reversed and is invalid for append.

concepts.heading: Deduplication Without a Watermark
concepts.body: Deduplicating a stream means remembering the keys already seen, because a new row can only be recognized as a repeat against history. That memory is streaming state, kept on the executors and saved in the checkpoint. Without a watermark, `streamingDf.dropDuplicates(["guid"])` works like batch deduplication on a unique identifier. Because a duplicate might arrive at any time, Spark stores every `guid` it has seen, with no time-based cleanup. The result is exact across the whole history, but state grows without bound and eventually causes memory pressure on a query that runs for months. This choice is right only when the key space is small, or when exact lifetime-wide uniqueness is required and the state cost is acceptable. The deduplication columns of a running query cannot be changed on restart, so decide the key before you start. Note that `distinct()` is not supported on streams; `dropDuplicates` is the supported way.

concepts.heading: Deduplication With a Watermark
concepts.body: If there is an upper bound on how late a duplicate can arrive, put the event time into the key. The documented pattern is `withWatermark("eventTime", "10 seconds").dropDuplicates(["guid", "eventTime"])`. Spark can drop state only when an entry's event time is older than the watermark, so the key `guid` alone would not let the watermark clean anything. The watermark must be defined before the deduplication. This requires duplicates to carry the same event time as the original. When they do not, for example a replayed record stamped at write time, use `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["guid"])`, added in Spark 3.5. It needs a watermark on the DataFrame, but the event-time column need not be in the key. Copies are removed while their time distance is below the delay threshold, so set the threshold longer than the largest gap between duplicates: with 1 hour, a copy 3 hours later passes as new. Data older than the watermark is dropped, even if its `guid` is new.

examPoints: Sliding windows overlap, so an event at 12:07 with a 10-minute window sliding every 5 minutes is counted twice; session windows grow with activity and do not support update mode.
`withWatermark` goes before the aggregation on the same event-time column; append mode emits a window only after the watermark passes it, and watermark is max event time minus the threshold.

No watermark means dropDuplicates state grows forever; with a watermark use guid plus event time, or dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(guid) when event times differ, with a threshold above the largest gap.

quiz.q: A query uses `window("ts", "10 minutes", "5 minutes")`. In how many windows is an event with `ts` of 12:13 counted?
choices: One window, 12:10 to 12:20, because each event is assigned to the window starting closest to it
Three windows, 12:00 to 12:10, 12:05 to 12:15 and 12:10 to 12:20, because the slide adds one extra window
Zero windows, because windowed counts are held back until the watermark has passed the event time
Two windows, 12:05 to 12:15 and 12:10 to 12:20
quiz.explain: Windows start every 5 minutes and last 10. 12:13 lies in 12:05-12:15 and 12:10-12:20, and past the end of 12:00-12:10.

quiz.q: Duplicates of an event can arrive up to 30 minutes after the first copy, with the same `guid` but a different `event_time`. Which query bounds the deduplication state?
choices: `events.dropDuplicates(["guid"])`, because Spark removes `guid` values from state after the longest trigger interval
`events.withWatermark("event_time", "1 hour").dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["guid"])`
`events.withWatermark("event_time", "1 hour").dropDuplicates(["guid", "event_time"])`, since the event time in the key lets the watermark clean the state
`events.dropDuplicates(["guid"]).withWatermark("event_time", "1 hour")`, because a watermark added later trims the state
quiz.explain: Copies have different event times, so adding event time to the key would miss them. The within-watermark variant keys on guid alone and still needs a watermark before it, set above the 30-minute gap.

recap: Windows come in tumbling, sliding and session forms. A watermark is max event time minus the delay and must precede the aggregation. Deduplication without a watermark keeps state forever; with one, key on guid plus event time or use dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark.
